lesson.title: What you type can travel
lesson.subtitle: Where your words go, and what to keep out

video.title: What you type can travel
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Cards: Names and marks; A health note; Where would it go?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Last term I nearly pasted my whole class list into a chatbot. Names, marks, and a note about one girl's health, just to get help writing reports. I stopped, and asked myself: where would those words go?

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: what happens to what you type, and how to get help without giving your pupils away.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: When you send a prompt, it leaves your phone. It goes to the company's servers, and it may be kept in your chat history. Some services let staff read samples to check quality. And unless you switch it off, some use chats to train future models.

scenes.visual: A list: A shared phone keeps the history; The next person can read it; A shared chat link opens for anyone.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Then there's the phone itself. A shared phone or staffroom computer keeps the history open for the next person. And a chat shared as a link opens for anyone who gets it.

scenes.visual: Cards: Before you type; On the noticeboard?; Yes: fine; No: keep it out.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: So here's a simple test. Before you type something, ask: would I pin this on the staffroom noticeboard? If not, it doesn't go into a chatbot either.

scenes.visual: A list: Green: no person in it; Amber: names and details out; Red: never type it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Think of it as a traffic light. Green has no person in it, like “a Primary Five class of sixty, with no lab”. Amber is fine only with names and details taken out, like “Pupil A finds fractions hard”. Red never goes in: names with marks or health, passwords, or an exam before the exam.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! I want help writing a report for a pupil who often misses school because of an illness. What do I type?

scenes.visual: Two columns. Red: keep out: Her full name; Her illness. Type this: “A pupil”; “Often absent”; Add the name later.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The second one. The chatbot needs the situation, not the child. “A pupil who often misses school for health reasons” gets you the same help, and gives nothing away. You add the name yourself, later, on paper.

scenes.visual: A list: Turn off history or training; Use the school's approved tool; Sign out on shared devices.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Check the settings too. Many tools let you turn off chat history or training, and some school accounts promise not to use your data. Use the tool your school has approved, and sign out on shared devices.

scenes.visual: A list: Photos can show names; Cover the name; Or type the words.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In my school we added one more rule. Photos count too: a picture of marked work often shows a name. Cover the name, or type the words out instead.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Role and task; Context; Format; No names needed.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: build a better prompt
scenes.narration: In the app, build a prompt from parts: role, task, context and format. Watch the answer improve as you add context. And notice: useful context never needs a child's name.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A colleague wants a chatbot to write a letter home about a fight in class. Which version is safe to type?

scenes.visual: The summary: Your words travel; The noticeboard test; The situation, not the child; Check the settings. Takeaway: Help for your class never needs your pupils' secrets.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: The second one: the situation is enough for a calm letter. Remember: your words travel to servers and histories. Use the noticeboard test, share the situation, not the child, and check the settings.

scenes.visual: A list: Read out what people type; Green, amber or red card; Say why; One class rule.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: play “Green, amber, red”. Read out things someone might type into an app. Pupils hold up a green, amber or red card, and say why. Finish with one rule the class will keep.

checkpoints.prompt: A pupil often misses school because of an illness. What do you type to get help with her report?

options.text: Her full name, her illness and her marks
“A pupil who often misses school for health reasons”
Nothing: AI can never help with reports

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: keep the situation, leave out who it is. The help is just as good.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: her name and illness are red. Describe the situation without the child.

checkpoints.prompt: A colleague wants a chatbot to draft a letter home about a fight in class. Which is safe to type?

options.text: The pupils' names and what each one did
“Two pupils had a fight; write a calm letter to parents”
A photo of the incident report

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Yes: the situation is enough for a calm letter. Add the names yourself.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: names and the report are red. Describe the situation and add names yourself.
